_comment: m1 balanced, with the agent class's SLO restated for a policy that cannot
express an end-to-end budget.
The agent class's real SLO is E2E <= 30 s, and the analysis scores it that way
whatever this file says. FluidServe is told so directly (25:e2e:30000) and
derives a nominal pace of 30,000 / 520.2 measured output tokens = 57.7 ms per
token. Llumnix's own SLO policy has no end-to-end mode: it takes tbt_ms
literally as a per-token target. With the default decomposition (11,800, 25) it
therefore judged the agent class at 25 ms per token -- 2.3x tighter than
FluidServe judged the same requests -- and refused every instance, rejecting
98% of that class.
This file gives it the decomposition closest to FluidServe's nominal pace that
still fits the 30 s budget at the measured output length:
It is not an equivalent statement of the same SLO, and cannot be: an end-to-end
budget allows trading time to first token against per-token pace, and a fixed
(ttft, tbt) pair fixes one point on that trade. That is the limitation under
test. This file makes the baseline as strong as a static pair can be, so that
what remains is the limitation and not the configuration.
chat and deep research are unchanged: their SLOs are natively (ttft, tbt).

mean_input_tokens is MEASURED at the gateway, not estimated by the transcript builder. The agent class was declared 6,812 from a tiktoken pass over the transcript file while the runtime actually sends 5,557, and deep research moved 4,055 -> 4,639 when its system prompt grew and its notes became the question's own. The request-count ratios below are NOT retuned to restore the old token shares: the trace files and every earlier run encode those counts, and changing the workload and the mix in the same step would make the two indistinguishable. Realised input token shares with these means: m1 30/43/26, m2 64/23/14, m3 20/24/57.
